query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In HEA protective coatings, wear resistance is primarily enhanced by controlled precipitation strengthening. When a small deviation from perfect stoichiometry induces the formation of nanoscale, hard L21-type precipitates dispersed in a softer BCC matrix, these precipitates act as load-bearing centers and serve to pin dislocations, thereby reducing plastic deformation and wear. In contrast, coatings with strictly stoichiometric compositions form continuous antiphase domains (APDs) that do not offer the same wear resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: HEA protective coating with near-ideal stoichiometry that tends to form ordered APDs within a BCC matrix.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled compositional deviation from the stoichiometric ratio (within the Al <25 at.% and Mn >15 at.% range) to promote the formation of discrete nanoscale L21 precipitates instead of continuous APDs.
generation.conditions: Wear tests under controlled abrasion (e.g., pin‐on‐disk) at room temperature to moderately elevated temperatures (<700 °C) using consistent loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and distribution of nanoscale (10–30 nm) L21 precipitates within a BCC matrix versus a predominantly APD microstructure.
generation.mechanism: The discrete precipitates bear a higher portion of the load (load-transfer effect) and also inhibit dislocation motion by acting as effective barriers. This dual effect reduces local plastic deformation under abrasive conditions, thereby improving the wear resistance of the coating compared to a microstructure with continuous APDs.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings engineered to form nanoscale L21 precipitates will exhibit higher hardness, lower wear rates, and reduced plastic deformation under identical wear testing conditions compared to coatings with stoichiometric compositions exhibiting APDs.
generation.baseline: A coating with a nearly stoichiometric composition that predominantly develops APDs in the BCC matrix without discrete precipitate formation.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to hold within the compositional range where small deviations (e.g., in Al and Mn contents) favor the formation of L21 precipitates; its benefits are anticipated under moderate wear loading and temperature conditions typical of protective coatings.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between precipitate size/density and the magnitude of wear resistance improvement is not yet fully established. Additionally, the potential interference from other strengthening mechanisms (e.g., grain boundary effects) introduces some uncertainty in attributing wear performance solely to precipitate formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA protective coatings: one set with the near-stoichiometric composition that forms predominantly APDs, and another set with a slight compositional deviation engineered to form nanoscale L21 precipitates. Confirm microstructures using TEM. Subject both sets to identical wear tests (e.g., pin‐on‐disk abrasion tests) under controlled load, sliding speed, and temperature conditions. Compare wear rates, hardness, and friction coefficients.
measurements: Wear rate (mass loss per unit sliding distance)
Microstructural analysis (TEM imaging of precipitate size and distribution)
Coefficient of friction during wear tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coatings with engineered precipitates do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in hardness and lower wear rates compared to the APD-based coatings, or if no clear correlation between precipitate distribution and wear resistance is observed, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How can high-throughput computational screening be used to discover lightweight, precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloys with high-temperature strength superior to traditional ferritic superalloys?. System: Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system (specifically Al20Cr5Fe50Mn20Ti5 and Al15Cr5Fe50Mn25Ti5 as successful cases). Processing: Arc-melting of 99.9 wt% purity constituent elements, melted at least six times for homogeneity, followed by drop-casting; subsequent homogenization at 1200 °C and annealing at 700 °C for 2 hours for specific characterizations. Test conditions: Compression tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 700 °C) at a strain rate of 2 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; in situ neutron scattering from room temperature to 1050 °C; synchrotron XRD and TEM characterization.
